title: Compound verbs
intro: A compound verb (*birleşik fiil*) joins a verb stem and a second verb through a vowel: *aç-ıver-*, *bak-akal-*, *yi-y-edur-*. The second verb loses most of its own meaning and adds a shade: quickly, frozen in place, carry on, almost, for ages. You have used one since A2: `-(y)Abil` grew out of *bilmek* ([A2 unit 5](gp-abil)). This unit adds four more, all written as one word, and two patterns with `-(y)Ip` that stay two words: `-(y)Ip durmak` and `-(y)Ip kalmak`.

blocks.text: `-(y)Iver` makes an action quick, easy or unexpected. Take the stem, add a vowel in four-way harmony (with the buffer y after a vowel), then *vermek*: *aç-* → *açıver-*, *oku-* → *okuyuver-*. Tense and person go on *ver-*, exactly as on the verb *vermek*: *açıverdim*, *açıveriyor*, *açıverir misin?*

**Three uses.** First, something done quickly and without effort: *Yemeği on dakikada hazırlayıverdi* (She whipped up the meal in ten minutes). Second, something sudden or unexpected, often with *birden* or *bir anda*: *Kapı birden açılıverdi* (The door suddenly swung open). Third, and most often in conversation, a request that sounds small and friendly: *Şu kapıyı açıverir misin?* (Could you just open that door?), *Bir bakıver* (Have a quick look).

blocks.caption: Question and negative
head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: did you have a quick look?
just don't go, just skip it

blocks.text: **Negatives are rare.** A quick action is usually a positive one. To say **he didn't open it**, Turkish just says *açmadı*. The negative on *ver-* (*bakıvermedi*) is possible but unusual. In speech you will also hear the negative inside, before `-(y)Iver`, for **just don't**: *Bugün işe gitmeyiver* (Just skip work today).

items.en: Could you just pass me that bag?
She whipped up the meal in ten minutes.
The door suddenly swung open.
items.note: Passive *-ıl* first, then `-(y)Iver`: no one opened it, it just opened.

items.tr: Bir bakıver, bu adres doğru mu?
items.seg: Bir bak|ıver, bu adres doğru mu?
items.en: Have a quick look: is this address right?
When the child fell, she burst into tears.
On the way, I suddenly ran into an old friend.

blocks.text: Write `-(y)Iver` as part of the verb: *açıver*, *okuyuver*, never *açı ver*. And keep it apart from the real verb *vermek*: *Kitabı verdi* (He gave the book) against *Kitabı okuyuverdi* (He read the book in no time).

In requests `-(y)Iver` works like English **just** (*Could you just…?*): it makes the favour sound small. For the quick-and-easy sense, French has **vite fait**: *Bir bakıver* is close to **jette un coup d'œil vite fait**.

`-(y)Akal` (the stem, `-(y)A`, then *kalmak*) leaves someone stuck in a state, usually from surprise or shock, or describes something that happened without meaning to. It isn't productive: it lives in a handful of verbs, each written as one word and listed in the dictionary.

head: Verb
Meaning
Example
rows: to be left stranded, left standing
to fall asleep without meaning to; to oversleep

blocks.text: The negative and the question are regular, on *kal-*: *Uyuyakalmadım, trafiğe takıldım* (I didn't oversleep, I got stuck in traffic), *Yine mi uyuyakaldın?* (Did you oversleep again?). Since these verbs tell what happened to you, they are mostly in the past, or in `-mIş` when you only realize it afterwards ([B1 unit 3](gp-mis-vs-di)): *Televizyonun karşısında uyuyakalmışım* (I must have dozed off in front of the TV).

items.en: When I opened the door, I just stood there staring.
When she heard the news, she froze.

items.tr: Fiyatın bu kadar yüksek olmasına şaşakaldık.
items.seg: Fiyatın bu kadar yüksek olmasına şaş|akal|dı|k.
items.en: We were dumbfounded that the price was so high.
My friends left, and I was left standing at the door.
I must have dozed off in front of the TV.

blocks.text: *Uyuyakalmak* isn't just **to sleep**. *Dün gece sekiz saat uyudum* is a plain fact; *Toplantıda uyuyakaldım* means you fell asleep when you shouldn't have.

`-(y)Adur` (the stem, `-(y)A`, then *durmak*) means **carry on, keep on meanwhile**. Its home is the imperative and the optative: you tell people to go on with something while you do something else, or you say you'll go ahead. It is written as one word, and the endings go on *dur-*.

blocks.title: *gidedurmak*: let me go on ahead, go on ahead…

rows.en: let him or her go on ahead

blocks.text: The forms are the imperative of [A1 unit 12](gp-imperative), the optative of [A2 unit 7](gp-optative) and the third-person imperative, all on *dur-*. The negative is the plain negative of the main verb: *Beni beklemeyin, başlayın* (Don't wait for me, start). A host says *Siz yiyedurun, ben de geliyorum* (Go ahead and eat, I'm coming too); a friend says *Sen anlatadur, ben çay koyayım* (Keep talking, I'll put the kettle on).

**With -ken.** `-(y)Adururken` is **while (all the while)**, for something that goes on as something else happens: *Biz konuşadururken otobüs çoktan gitmişti* (While we stood there talking, the bus had long gone). This use is more written.

items.en: Go ahead and eat, I'm coming too.
Keep talking, I'll put the kettle on.

items.tr: Siz başlayadurun, ben beş dakika sonra geliyorum.
items.seg: Siz başla|y|adur|un, ben beş dakika sonra geliyorum.
items.en: Start without me, I'll be there in five minutes.
I'll go on ahead, you follow.
While we stood there talking, the bus had long gone.

blocks.text: On its own *durmak* is **to stop**; inside `-(y)Adur` it means the opposite, **carry on**. *Siz yiyedurun* never means **stop eating**.
`-(y)Adur` is kind: it lets someone go on. `-(y)Ip durmak` (below) is a complaint about something that won't stop: *Siz yiyedurun* against *Sürekli yiyip duruyorsun* (You keep eating all the time).

sections.title: Düşeyazdım, süregelen: almost, and for ages

blocks.text: `-(y)Ayaz` (the stem, `-(y)A`, then *yazmak*) is **almost, very nearly**: something that came close to happening and didn't. It is used with a few verbs of falling, fainting and dying, almost always in the past and in the positive, and it sounds a little literary or playful.

head: Compound verb
Meaning
Everyday equivalent
rows: we nearly died (of fright, of laughter)

blocks.text: In conversation, a near miss is usually *az kalsın* ([B1 unit 2](b1-u02)) or *neredeyse* with the past continuous: *Az kalsın düşüyordum* (I nearly fell). *Az kalsın düşecektim*, with the future in the past, is just as common.

`-(y)Agel` (the stem, `-(y)A`, then *gelmek*) is the opposite in time: something that **has gone on for a long time, has always been done**. It belongs to formal and written Turkish, and its favourite forms are participles: *süregelen* (long-standing, ongoing), *olagelen* (that has always happened), *yapılagelen* (customary). The verbs are written as one word: *süregelmek*, *olagelmek*.

items.en: I slipped on the ice and almost fell.
We nearly died laughing.
Simit is a tradition that has gone on for centuries.

items.tr: Bu konuda yıllardır süregelen bir tartışma var.
items.seg: Bu konuda yıllardır sür|egel|en bir tartışma var.
items.en: There has been a debate about this for years.

items.tr: Köyde eskiden beri yapılagelen bir düğün geleneği bu.
items.seg: Köyde eskiden beri yap|ıl|agel|en bir düğün geleneği bu.
items.en: This is a wedding custom that has long been kept in the village.

blocks.text: `-(y)Agel` often stands next to a duration with `-DIr` or *beri*: *yüzyıllardır süregelen*, *eskiden beri yapılagelen*. In speech you would say *yüzyıllardır devam eden*.

sections.title: Söyleyip durma! Over and over, and stuck

blocks.text: Two verbs joined by `-(y)Ip` ([A2 unit 11](gp-ip)) can work as one. With *durmak*, the action happens **over and over, without stopping**, and the speaker is often annoyed: *Aynı şeyi söyleyip duruyorsun* (You keep saying the same thing). Tense and person go on *durmak*; the two words stay apart.

blocks.title: *söyleyip durmak*, present continuous: I keep saying

blocks.text: The negative imperative tells someone to stop: *Söyleyip durma!* (Stop going on about it!). The question asks why: *Neden bana bakıp duruyorsun?* (Why do you keep looking at me?). In the past it tells what went on and on: *Bütün gece öksürüp durdu* (He kept coughing all night).

With *kalmak*, `-(y)Ip kalmak` means **ending up stuck** in a state: *donup kaldım* (I froze), *şaşırıp kaldık* (we were stunned), *trafikte sıkışıp kaldık* (we got stuck in traffic), *bir soruya takılıp kaldım* (I got stuck on a question). It overlaps with `-(y)Akal` (*donakaldım* = *donup kaldım*), but it works with many more verbs.

items.en: He kept coughing all night.
Stop saying the same thing over and over!
Why do you keep looking at me?
We got stuck in traffic.
I got stuck on the first question in the exam.

blocks.title: Kapıp kaçtı, kalkıp gitti
blocks.text: Other everyday pairs with `-(y)Ip` behave like one verb: *kapıp kaçmak* (to snatch and run), *kalkıp gitmek* (to get up and leave), *çıkıp gelmek* (to turn up out of the blue). *Kedi balığı kapıp kaçtı* (The cat grabbed the fish and ran).

summary: A compound verb joins a stem, a linking vowel and a second verb, written as one word: *açıver-*, *bakakal-*, *gidedur-*, *düşeyaz-*, *süregel-*. Tense and person go on the second verb.
`-(y)Iver` is quick, easy or sudden, and makes requests friendly: *Bir bakıver*, *Şunu tutuverir misin?*, *Kapı birden açılıverdi*.
`-(y)Akal` is frozen in a state: *bakakaldım*, *donakaldı*, *şaşakaldık*, *kalakaldık*, *uyuyakaldım* (I overslept).
`-(y)Adur` is **carry on**, mostly in the imperative and optative: *Siz yiyedurun*, *Ben gidedurayım*.
`-(y)Ayaz` is a literary **almost** (*düşeyazdım*; everyday *az kalsın düşüyordum*); `-(y)Agel` is **long-standing**, mostly in *süregelen*.
`-(y)Ip durmak` is **keep doing**, often a complaint (*Söyleyip durma!*); `-(y)Ip kalmak` is **end up stuck** (*trafikte sıkışıp kaldık*).
